# Building an arrangement {#sec-arrangement}

Tracks describe simultaneous parts; sections describe successive parts of
the piece. A section spans every track, so moving a chorus means moving its
bass, melody, controllers and tempo changes together. Working within a track
instead changes one part while the surrounding arrangement stays aligned.

This distinction gives Modal two scales of structural editing: music within
a section and sections within the song.

## Bars, tracks and sections

In the arrangement, the cursor's bar belongs to its track. The section strip
above the tracks belongs to the whole song. `gs`, “go to section strip”,
changes the focus to that structure. Down (or `j`) moves back down from the
strip to the track rows. This is ordinary downward movement, not a separate
shortcut to memorise. Up (or `k`) from the first track moves back onto the strip.
On the strip, left and right move between sections rather than bars.

`is`, **in section**, follows this context. On a track it means that track's
events in the section; on the strip it means the section's events on every
track. `as`, **around section**, is available on the strip for the section
itself. Consequently `dis` on the strip clears its music but leaves its
time, while `das` removes the section and shortens the song.

A section copy is independent after it is put. It is a convenient way to
start a second verse from the first, without linking their subsequent edits.
Sections are not reusable patterns with shared content.

## Giving the song structure

A new song begins with one track and a section. Naming sections for their
musical roles makes navigation and copying easier. The section commands
live under `, s`; their actions apply to the cursor's section from other
views too.

| Intention | On the section strip | From anywhere in the song |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rename the section | `c` | `, s r` |
| Insert a section before / after | `i` / `a` | `, s i` / `, s a` |
| Join with the next section | `J` | `, s j` |
| Start a section at the current bar | — | `, s s` |
| Edit name and length | `e` | — |
| Add / remove a bar of section length | `+` / `-` | — |

The leader commands also work while the strip has focus. “Anywhere in the
song” means the arrangement, its strip, the piano roll or the event list;
the Ports and other settings pages do not provide that section context.

The last two controls are specific to a section focused on the strip:
`e` edits that section's fields, and `+` / `-` change its length. They have
no default leader binding. `ga` opens the arrangement and `gs` focuses its
strip, where those controls have their section-editing meaning.

The distinction between inserting **before** and adding **after** is also
a useful mnemonic for `i` and `a` here. These are section commands in this
context, not the prefixes of an object awaiting an operator.

Splitting an existing section at a bar line gives the later material a new
section without moving its notes in time. `:section-split NAME` names that
new part; `, s s` invokes the same command and asks for the name.
Joining performs the complementary structural operation. Section
names are unique; copies gain a numbered suffix so a named destination
remains unambiguous.

## Copying and rearranging whole sections

On the strip, `Y` yanks the current section and `x` deletes it. Operators
with motions can take several sections. `p` puts whole sections after the
cursor's section; `P` puts them before. Their lengths and the material on
all tracks go together.

`Alt-h` and `Alt-l` (or Alt-Left and Alt-Right) move a section earlier or
later through its neighbours. Reordering changes
its position in the piece, while preserving the relative timing inside it.
A section's labels and its local tempo and meter information travel with it.
Enter on the strip plays from that section, allowing its musical role to
be heard in context.

The strip's `ie` object means the entire song's events on every track.
Its breadth is intentional: a whole-song edit is made from the place that
represents the whole structure, rather than accidentally reaching every
track from a single part.

## Copying music without changing the structure

On arrangement tracks and in the piano roll, `p` merges copied events over
what is there. `P` inserts the copied time, moving later material **within
the section**; it asks before growing a section when necessary. On a Visual
selection, either key replaces the selection as one change.

Copied bars go to the start of the destination bar. Other event material
goes to the cursor's time. The message after a put states what was put,
where, and whether it merged, inserted or replaced material.

In the piano roll, Alt-P and Alt-p add pitch placement to the corresponding
put. Intervals are preserved relative to the pitch at which the material
was taken, so a melodic shape can start on another note. `:put-ending`
anchors the copy's end at the cursor instead of its start: useful for a
lead-in that must arrive at a downbeat. It has no default key binding;
the command line, palette or a personal binding provides access to it.

A register can hold events, whole tracks or sections. These are different
kinds of material, not interchangeable clipboard formats. A section copy
belongs on the strip. A whole-track copy becomes new tracks: `p` and `P` put
it after or before the current track, here as in the Tracks view. Named registers
for keeping several copies are covered in @sec-efficient-work.

## Removing contents, removing time

Clearing a bar and closing a gap are different musical decisions. `dib`
removes the events starting in the bar and leaves silence. `dab` removes
that bar as time on the chosen track, closing up the remainder of its
section. Later sections remain aligned.

A Visual `D` removes the selection's time, also closing up within each
section. In the piano roll it requires time at every pitch: a pitch box
would leave unclear what should happen to unselected notes crossing it.
The event list refuses this time-removal operation.

To change the song's length across every track, `:bar-delete` (`, b d`) and
`:bar-insert` (`, b i`) are explicit alternatives. They use the conductor's bars.
For example, `:bar-insert 2 3/4` adds two empty bars of 3/4 before the cursor's
bar. A deleted run is kept as section material that can be put on the strip.

Events are normally taken by their starts. A note beginning before a selected
range can therefore cross into it without becoming a target. The `|` command
cuts notes at selection boundaries so only the pieces inside are taken;
placed before an operator, it applies to that edit, as in `|d]b`.

## Labels describe places without dividing the song

A **label** is a named position. Unlike a section boundary, it need not divide
the arrangement: “bass entry” or “check this transition” can simply identify
a place. `, l l` (`:label NAME`) creates or renames one at the cursor, asking
for its name; `, l d` (`:label-delete`) removes one there, or all labels in a
Visual range. `[l` and `]l` navigate between labels. The `, l` group,
**labels and marks**, gathers these with the marks' commands.

An imported MIDI file may contain labels that already describe its form.
`:label-to-section` (`, s l`, or `, l s`) converts the label at or before the cursor into
a section boundary at its bar line. On a selection, it converts the labels in that
range. Off-bar labels ask for confirmation because the structural boundary
will be at the bar line rather than the label's exact time.

This allows labels to serve first as observations, and later as structure
when the intended divisions are settled.

## Meter counts time; rebarring does not move notes

The **conductor** supplies the song's tempo and reference meter. A track
normally follows that meter, but can have a meter of its own in a section.
The same elapsed musical time might therefore be three bars on one track
and four on another. Arrangement columns represent time, not a promise
that every track's bar numbers line up.

The ruler uses the conductor's bars; the cursor and its position display use
the current track's. Bars with an independent meter have a tint, and the track
bar shows `own` after its meter. `, T b` toggles the tint. The piano roll
shows the current track's meters along its own ruler.

Without a selection, `:meter 3/4`, or `, b m` followed by the meter, inserts
a meter from the cursor to the next meter change or the section's end.
It affects the meter the current track follows: the conductor's
or its own. It never shifts notes. A change inside a bar first makes a short
remainder bar where necessary.

**Rebarring** applies a meter to a selected span and restores the earlier
meter afterwards. `:rebar 3/4`, also reached with `, b m` in Visual mode,
counts that time in threes without stretching the music. Ten quarter-note
beats become three 3/4 bars and one 1/4 remainder bar.

The selection determines whose bars change:

- A `v` range in the arrangement, or sections on the strip, changes the
  conductor and tracks following it. Tracks with their own meter keep it.
- A track box or `V` rows changes only those tracks, giving them a meter
  of their own. In the piano roll or event list the selected rebar affects
  the displayed track.

Meter ownership is per whole section. Rebarring part of one track's section
therefore gives it its own meter throughout that section, copying the
conductor's meter outside the changed span. Subsequent conductor changes
will no longer reach it there.

`:meter follow` (`, s f`) returns the current track to following the conductor
in the current section. On a selection, it requires exact whole sections. That
requirement reflects what is being changed: ownership of the section's
meter, rather than just the appearance of a few bar lines.
